title: Why must you synchronize both sides of a bidirectional relationship in JPA? What helper methods solve this, and what goes wrong if you do not?
shortTitle: Synchronize both sides of a bidirectional relationship — helper methods and what goes wrong

s1_definition.profdef: In a bidirectional JPA association, two fields model the same relationship — for example a `Portfolio` has a `List<Holding>` and each `Holding` has a `Portfolio` reference. Only one side is the **owning side** (the one with the foreign-key column, usually the `@ManyToOne`); the other is the **inverse side** marked `mappedBy`. Hibernate persists the relationship based solely on the owning side. If you update only one side in memory, the object graph becomes inconsistent: the in-memory model disagrees with the database, and lazy reloads behave unexpectedly. The fix is **helper methods** on the parent (such as `addHolding`/`removeHolding`) that set both sides together, keeping the in-memory graph consistent.
s1_definition.analogy: A portfolio and its holdings are like a manager and their team members. The relationship has two views: the manager's list of team members, and each member's "my manager" field. If you add a member to the manager's list but forget to set that member's manager field, the org chart becomes self-contradictory — the manager thinks they have five reports, but one of those reports thinks they have no manager. The bank's HR system (the database) only trusts the "my manager" field (the owning side), so the manager's list in memory can be a lie. Helper methods are like a single HR form that updates both views at once so they never disagree.
s1_definition.oneliner: Only the owning side (the foreign key) is persisted; update both sides via helper methods so the in-memory object graph stays consistent with the database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In a bidirectional JPA association, two fields model the same relationship — for example a `Portfolio` has a `List<Holding>` and each `Holding` has a `Portfolio` reference. Only one side is the **owning side** (the one with the foreign-key column, usually the `@ManyToOne`); the other is the **inverse side** marked `mappedBy`. Hibernate persists the relationship based solely on the owning side. If you update only one side in memory, the object graph becomes inconsistent: the in-memory model disagrees with the database, and lazy reloads behave unexpectedly. The fix is **helper methods** on the parent (such as `addHolding`/`removeHolding`) that set both sides together, keeping the in-memory graph consistent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A portfolio and its holdings are like a manager and their team members. The relationship has two views: the manager's list of team members, and each member's "my manager" field. If you add a member to the manager's list but forget to set that member's manager field, the org chart becomes self-contradictory — the manager thinks they have five reports, but one of those reports thinks they have no manager. The bank's HR system (the database) only trusts the "my manager" field (the owning side), so the manager's list in memory can be a lie. Helper methods are like a single HR form that updates both views at once so they never disagree.

**One line to remember:** Only the owning side (the foreign key) is persisted; update both sides via helper methods so the in-memory object graph stays consistent with the database.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — new holdings were saved with a null portfolio id.** At National Bank of India, a developer added a Holding to the portfolio's list but forgot to set the holding's portfolio reference, so the owning side was null and the database stored `portfolio_id = null`, detaching the holding from its portfolio. This is exactly the owning-side mistake.

**Problem 2 — the portfolio total was wrong in the same request.** Another path set the holding's portfolio (owning side) but never added it to the in-memory list, so a total computed by iterating the list missed the new holding within that transaction. This is exactly the stale-inverse-side mistake.

What the code will do: a `Portfolio` with proper `addHolding`/`removeHolding` helpers that set both sides, and a `PortfolioService` that uses them so both the database and the in-memory graph are always correct, plus logs demonstrating a consistent count and total.

# Run

# Add a holding (both sides synchronized)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/portfolios/PF-001/holdings \

sections.s5_journey:
Input: add INFY (80 shares at 1500) to portfolio PF-001, which already has some holdings.

Step 1 — `findById` loads PF-001 as managed. Its holdings load lazily when accessed.

Step 2 — a new Holding for INFY is created, still transient and not linked to any portfolio.

Step 3 — `pf.addHolding(h)` runs the helper: it adds the holding to the in-memory list (inverse side) and calls `h.setPortfolio(pf)` (owning side). Both views now agree.

Step 4 — because the owning side's portfolio reference is set, Hibernate will write the correct `portfolio_id` at flush; the NOT NULL foreign key is satisfied. `CascadeType.ALL` persists the new holding.

Step 5 — within the same transaction, `holdingCount()` and `totalValue()` iterate the in-memory list, which already includes INFY, so the count and total are correct immediately. Had we only set the owning side, the list would be stale and the total would miss INFY.

Step 6 — commit writes the holding with the correct foreign key; a later reload matches exactly what the code saw.

```
2026-10-24 01:19:02 INFO  Added INFY; count=3 total=360000.00
2026-10-24 01:19:02 DEBUG Hibernate: insert into holdings (portfolio_id, symbol, quantity, price) values (?,?,?,?)
```

```
  addHolding(PF-001, INFY, 80, 1500)
    │
    ▼
  findById → Portfolio (managed)
    │
  new Holding(INFY)  (transient, portfolio=null)
    │
    ▼
  pf.addHolding(h)
    ├─ holdings.add(h)        ← inverse side (in-memory list)
    └─ h.setPortfolio(pf)     ← OWNING side (FK) ← this persists
    │
    ▼
  flush → INSERT holdings(portfolio_id=PF-001, ...)  FK correct ✓
    │
    ▼
  totalValue()/count() over list → INCLUDES INFY ✓ (consistent in-TX)

  ── Broken variants ──
  only list.add → FK null → NOT NULL violation / detached holding ✗
  only setPortfolio → DB ok but list stale → wrong count/total in-TX ✗
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Owning vs Inverse Side (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Aggregate Root with encapsulated collection                │
  │  Tell-Don't-Ask: callers use addHolding, not raw list       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Portfolio owns relationship invariants                  │
  │  D: service depends on aggregate behavior, not raw setters  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐ 1   * ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Portfolio (inverse, mappedBy) │◆──────│ Holding (OWNING, FK)     │
  │ - holdings: List<Holding>     │       │ - portfolio: Portfolio   │
  │ + addHolding(h) sets BOTH     │       │ ~ setPortfolio(p) [pkg]  │
  │ + removeHolding(h) sets BOTH  │       │ + marketValue(): BigDec  │
  │ + getHoldings() unmodifiable  │       └──────────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── What persists (as prose) ──
  Hibernate writes the FK from the OWNING side (@ManyToOne) only.
  The mappedBy inverse list is ignored for persistence but used in-memory.

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. addHolding(service) → findById
  2. new Holding → pf.addHolding(h)
  3.   list.add (inverse) + setPortfolio (owning)
  4. flush → INSERT with correct FK
  5. count/total over list → consistent

  ⚠ Only list.add → null FK. ⚠ Only setPortfolio → stale list in-TX.
  ⚠ @ManyToMany: sync both collections. equals/hashCode on business key.
  Rule: mutate relationships only through helper methods that set both sides.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In a bidirectional relationship two fields model the same link, for example a portfolio has a list of holdings and each holding has a reference back to its portfolio, but only one side is the owning side and the other is the inverse side marked with mappedBy. The owning side is normally the many-to-one side because it holds the foreign key column, and Hibernate decides what to write to the database based solely on that owning side. The inverse mappedBy side is ignored for persistence, so if I update only the inverse side, the database foreign key is never set correctly.

This leads to two classic bugs. If I add a holding to the portfolio's list but forget to set the holding's portfolio reference, the owning side is null, so Hibernate writes a null foreign key or violates a not-null constraint, and the holding is effectively detached from its portfolio in the database even though my in-memory list claims otherwise. The reverse mistake is subtler: if I set the holding's portfolio but never add it to the portfolio's list, the database is correct, but within the same transaction the in-memory list is stale, so any count or total I compute by iterating that list silently misses the new holding.

The robust fix, which I apply everywhere at National Bank of India, is to expose helper methods on the aggregate root, such as addHolding and removeHolding, that set both sides together, and to make the owning-side setter package-private and return the collection as an unmodifiable view so callers cannot bypass the helpers. In our portfolio service we had both failure modes in production: holdings saved with a null portfolio id, and a wrong portfolio total within a request because the list was stale. After routing every mutation through helper methods, the database foreign key and the in-memory object graph always agree. The nuances I always mention are that for a many-to-many I synchronize both collections, that I implement equals and hashCode on a stable business key rather than the generated id to avoid problems before the id is assigned, and that orphan removal only behaves correctly when the collection state is kept consistent through these helpers.
